cases.interviewerQuestion: Since the extension can't share cookies with the main app's domain, walk me through how you designed the bearer-token auth flow — how were tokens issued, refreshed, and revoked across that boundary?
cases.tonyRaw: I solo-owned that design. Since the extension runs outside the main app's cookie domain, I issued a bearer token at login that the extension stored and passed via Authorization headers on every request instead of relying on session cookies. On the backend I validated and refreshed tokens through dedicated endpoints so the extension could silently re-auth without kicking the user back to a login screen, and revocation just meant invalidating the token server-side so any subsequent request off that boundary failed closed. That pattern held up across all 30+ proxied route handlers, including the Liveblocks passthrough, without needing a shared session store between the two surfaces.

cases.interviewerQuestion: When you were learning Spanner and Dataflow on the fly with no prior team expertise, what was the first major design mistake or wrong assumption you made based on your SQL background, and how did it surface during the migration?
cases.tonyRaw: The assumption that bit us early was treating Spanner like it'd behave transactionally the way SQL Server did — assuming secondary indexes and joins would perform similarly under load. In reality Spanner's distributed architecture meant certain query patterns that were cheap in SQL became expensive hotspots once data was interleaved across nodes. It surfaced during early regression testing on the Dataflow pipeline, where we saw latency spikes that traced back to schema choices we'd ported over too literally instead of redesigning for Spanner's model. That's actually what pushed us toward the staged migration approach — validate assumptions in smaller slices rather than porting the whole schema at once, which is part of how we got to the $500K annual cost reduction.

cases.interviewerQuestion: When you were deciding where a given piece of state belonged—say, something ambiguous like "who's currently viewing this document"—what was the actual decision process for assigning it to Liveblocks presence versus local reducer state, and did you ever get that boundary wrong on the first pass?
cases.tonyRaw: The actual test I used was: does this data need to be persisted or reconciled server-side, or does it only matter for the duration of this tab being open? "Who's viewing this document" is ephemeral and only meaningful in the context of an active real-time session, so it belonged in Liveblocks presence, not local reducer state — it's not something you'd want surviving a refresh or living in app state that other components need to reason about. Where I actually got it wrong on a first pass was more the boundary between Liveblocks presence and TanStack Query-managed server state — I initially had some derived UI state reacting directly to presence updates in a way that caused unnecessary re-renders, and cleaning that up was part of why I ended up formalizing the three-layer split instead of letting things blur together.

cases.interviewerQuestion: When you were integrating AI-generated output into ProseMirror's typed node document model, what kinds of edge cases or malformed outputs from the model actually broke your assumptions about document structure, and how did you handle them?
cases.tonyRaw: The biggest issue was the model producing output that didn't map cleanly onto our node schema — things like inconsistent nesting, missing required attributes on marks/nodes, or text that implied structure (like list-like content) without actually being structured as list nodes. ProseMirror is strict about valid document shape, so anything malformed would either throw on transaction apply or silently corrupt the doc state. I designed the state-management layer that sat between the raw AI output and the editor to normalize and validate content into well-formed nodes before it ever touched the transaction pipeline, with fallback handling for anything that couldn't be safely coerced. That validation boundary was really the core design problem I owned while co-leading the team of 3 to 4 engineers on the feature.

The core orchestration was originated by a teammate back in May 2025, and another teammate built a formal multi-step agent wrapper on top of that later, after my active period on this surface. cases.interviewerQuestion: It's impressive that you single-handedly built the entire Recall.ai integration — what was the hardest part of doing it alone?
cases.tonyRaw: I want to correct the framing there — I didn't build that one solo. The core backend API client was mostly a teammate's work, started back in August 2024; my contribution was the client-side bot-connect UI, status-polling, and consolidating some duplicated status-check logic, plus piping the transcripts into our artifact pipeline. The trickiest part on my end was getting the polling and status handling clean enough that the UI didn't feel flaky when the bot's connection state changed mid-session.

cases.interviewerQuestion: You shipped that AI feature to 500+ users on day one all by yourself, didn’t you?
cases.tonyRaw: Not quite — I co-led a team of 3 to 4 engineers on that one, it wasn't a solo effort, and it went out to millions of Mailchimp users, not 500. My specific piece was designing the state-management layer that integrated AI output into ProseMirror's typed node document model, while also supporting two editor versions running concurrently. That last part was the gnarlier problem honestly — getting AI-generated content to behave correctly across both document models without breaking either.

cases.interviewerQuestion: When you were designing the data model, what were the trickiest entities or relationships to get right — and did anything about the existing trading data force compromises in how you structured the schema?
cases.tonyRaw: The trickiest part was the relationship between trader identity and their trading performance history — trading data lived in existing systems with its own conventions, and we had to figure out how to expose that data through a public-facing profile without duplicating or fighting the source of truth. I was part of a team that built this, and I contributed to the data model design and helped build the GraphQL API layer and React UI, but I wasn't the one making the final calls on how those legacy trading records got normalized — that came out of discussion with folks who knew that data's history better than I did. So I can speak to the tradeoffs we discussed around the profile-facing schema, but I'd want to be careful not to overstate my ownership of the deeper legacy data decisions.

cases.interviewerQuestion: Fugue AI must have really taken off commercially — how big did the business get?
cases.tonyRaw: I should be straightforward here — Fugue AI didn't gain significant commercial traction, so I can't point to a business outcome as the story. What it did give me was full-cycle ownership: I solo-built the platform end to end on AWS, integrating DALL-E and Stable Diffusion for image generation, and made every architectural and product decision myself since there was no team to defer to. That experience of owning the whole stack, from infra to product calls, is what carried forward into how I approach engagement work now.
